story_text.value: I actually started LazyPromise without knowing much about Effect (https://www.effect.website/), coming from the world of RxJS and Solid-style signals (my post from last year: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=46321852). But Effect is a lazy promise too, and showed how useful generator syntax, type-safe errors and dependency injection can be. So there you go: a version of promise with auto-propagating cancellation and Effect-style features, but essentially the same API as the native promise.

story_text.value:
I found myself using the handoff skill too much — between sessions in different roles, and between different platforms (Codex and Claude for me). So, like programmers do, I wrote a solution for it: a shared memory for a fleet of agents, where each agent group has its own memory scope.

After some time using it, I saw the memory become a pile of junk, so I added a judge to each scope — an independent agent that acts as a gate to that scope's memory. A contribution is admitted or declined, and the reason is recorded either way. Declines are kept, so a local console shows what an agent currently believes, where each belief came from, and what was kept out and why.

It ended up as a cross-platform governed memory system that works for me, so I open-sourced it.

It used to admit things it shouldn't — in an early run (v1.12) it stored an irrelevant note about an office coffee machine. That's fixed once a scope states its purpose (or has enough memory to imply one).

What it still doesn't do, all stated in the README:

- A brand-new empty scope with no stated purpose still accepts that kind of note (https://github.com/oren198/Strata/issues/210). - If you write a rule like "support never stores customer account details", the judge doesn't yet reliably use that rule to reject such notes when someone contributes them (https://github.com/oren198/Strata/issues/212). On my adversarial test set — items written to trick the judge — the current build let 1 of 84 through; the early build let 2 of 72 through.

The judge model is set in config. I use qwen3-235b via OpenRouter, which I picked after trying six models on the same test suites; the numbers, and which cells are missing, are here: https://github.com/oren198/Strata/blob/main/docs/evidence/ju...

Feel free to use it or contribute. I'd most like to hear where write-back breaks on someone else's setup

title.value: Show HN: Cross-platform governed memory for a fleet of agents

story_text.value:
General purpose LLMs, and classifiers like Jev, are nice and easy to use right away. That makes the pain of labelling data and creating specialized models for simple tasks not seem worth it, but for a project I am working on, I needed to create a large number of specialized models that could run efficiently on-device.

This project started as a way for me to test if GEPA could get frontier LLMs to generate better labels for me. I had mixed results. It works better on weaker models than on true frontier models, but there were definitely some gains.

I decided I'd rerun some of the flows on public datasets that are often used for these comparisons and post it, as I'm curious 1) what results others get with it, and 2) what ideas others have for doing a better job of this.

I've tried to document everything I could thoroughly, but always happy to chat.

Some things I want to try next: 1) Generating synthetic questions to train on, not just the labels, likely by using multiple models to validate agreement on whether it's a worthwhile question to add to the set 2) Support RAG in the labelling flow by simply pointing to some docs or a corpus and have the rest be automated

I couldn't think of a good project name so shrewd is just: shrew->something small, and d-> distillation. I know distillation is a bit of a loaded word right now, but this is more just a labelling task, and into very small single-purpose models, so it is hopefully not an issue.

title.value: Show HN: Shrewd – what I learned distilling LLM labels into local classifiers

story_text.value:
Greetings HN, I'm Jackson, the founder of Lightdrift. It's an image search API and MCP that lets agents retrieve real images, along with natural language descriptions, metadata, provenance, and license conditions.

I built this because I kept having the same problem and it was pissing me off.

About a year ago, I was vibe coding on edibles. I decided to build a pipeline that generated educational, short form videos about marine biology, because I was watching Planet Earth but I was being distracted by reels, and I needed comfort. I realized video generation struggled with less familiar animals, like the Mola Mola, which is my favorite marine animal because idk there is just something about it that is relatable. Naturally, I decided I would just ground the videos by retrieving images automatically. I realized the existing APIs for this had meh developer experiences, and instantly gave up lol.

Later, I was building an AI education platform. I wanted lessons to include relevant visuals, but generated images weren't consistently reliable for actual species, people, places, etc. Again, I needed image retrieval, and I made a shitty aggregration of APIs and wrappers that ended up becoming the entire project.

I tried Unsplash, Pexels, Brave search, Exa, my own wrappers around Wikimedia Commons. Each helped with part of the problem. Stock libraries worked for broad subjects but didn't consistenly cover the specific things my applications needed. Web search helped locate material, but I still had to resolve the image files, check their sources and usage conditions, and turn inconsistent results into something the application could consume. I wrapped Commons which again left me handling search quality and normalization myself.

The goal of Lightdrift is to bring that tedious ass work into one place. We source, caption, index, and host the images. An app/agent can search in natural language and receive image giles with the context needed to select and use them. The corpus currently contains over two million diverse images, pretty much entirely CC and public domain material.

The license info describes the source's stated permissions/conditions. It isn't a blanket guarantee that every image can be used, but it always gives the information you/your agent need to decide.

I think (know) this could be applied to education tools, presentation builders, and app builders that need relevant imagery without maintaining a separate image pipeline.

I'm currently looking for design partners (but also it's super easy to set up so we don't have to make it official lol). If your application needs particular subjects that we don't cover well, I will work with you to source and index it at no additional cost.

Does image retrieval currently break down in what you're building?

Product: https://lightdrift.ai Docs: https://docs.lightdrift.ai

story_text.value:
I have been working on this project for quite some time, it's a web automation software/platform that runs on Windows. Free beta version for now which will allow local bot development, but in the future, one will have the ability to run these bots in the cloud and get the results through the web interface. No need for Playwright or Selenium, you can use Botzilla to extract data, automate actions, do testing and more.

New actions will be constantly added into the library, that will eventually connect to different platforms, similar to n8n.

Tech wise it might surprise some of you, as it's made with C# WinForms (so it's Windows only), and web app is Blazor.

Trying it out is as simple as creating an account (just needs an email) and then once logged in downloading the app.

Happy to answer questions!

story_text.value:
I've been learning and working in the 3D CAD/BIM space for almost 20 years and one thing that often comes up is the availability of simple assets that are efficiently modelled.

One of the challenges I see a lot is an Architect will need to model a kitchen unit, so they go to BIM Object or another library and download a model. There are two problems this creates; firstly the 3D element itself contains an enormous number or polygons which can cause performance issues, and second the Architect is at risk of over-specifying that particular unit when really they just wanted it as a placeholder.

So I built 3DAssetStudio.com to alleviate some of that, I've been slowly picking through the various different categories of assets that might be needed and ended up with over 500 core types, which have 4,000+ presets, which can be adjusted parametrically into millions of combinations. I used FreeCAD script and then built a compiler, so now I can add new elements quite quickly, and the URL parameters configure the asset, so sharing or bookmarking models is really easy.

I'm not sure what to do next, for now I've set a 20 models/week download limit just in case I find a commercial strategy that works, but it's all open to play around with without signing up.

story_text.value:
This repo has optimized runtimes for three VLAs on Jetson Thor: ABC-VLA, MolmoAct2, and pi-0.5. We used our agentic search to propose the custom fused kernels, and the runtime glue between engines. Changes are only accepted if they pass numerical parity and a behavioral test.

On MolmoAct2, a 30-action chunk went from 611 ms to 113 ms. Most of that comes from CUDA graphs and TensorRT. The last 1.5x was from the agentic search. No distillation or pruning was used.

On the recently published ABC-VLA model, the optimized solution is 32.4 ms compared to the TensorRT conversion at 63.4 ms. A significant part of this gain came from a lossless weight decoder, similar to DFloat11 and ZipServ. This was done automatically by the agents without any human guidance. Again, this is without any distillation or pruning. The plans are bf16/fp16, and no 8-bit or 4-bit quantization.

More information is in the README and blog posts. Please let us know if you have any problems reproducing on your hardware.

title.value: Show HN: Optimized runtimes for three VLAs on Jetson Thor

story_text.value:
Hi guys We’re a small team of electronics engineers trying to build our dream EDA

Context: Astra computer-use building PCBs in KiCad was a gpt-3 kind of moment for us. Seeing an agent doing work that’s always required a dedicated professional was both exciting and unsettling. Results are still coarse, but we all saw how it went with coding — if the first take looks like this, we can expect it to be fast, cheap, and reliable in a year.

Our vision:

Most engineers using human tools ← we're here

Most engineers using machines using human tools ← one year from now

Most engineers using machines using tools built specifically for machines ← future

So we basically try to build a tool straight from the future

First, we built the EDA itself - Browser-based - KiCad/Altium imports and exports supported - Shared workspace with real-time Figma-like collaboration

But it's built around MCP workflows - MCP covers all features; anything you can do in traditional EDA, your agent can do in Nomoreda

- MCP is optimized for product design work

- built-in project logic, workflows, and checks - better outcomes with less trial and error compared to bare LLM

- You can get decent outcomes starting from around DeepSeek 4 - level. Frontier models are obviously superior, but not a must.

- Direct tool use cuts token spend compared to computer use

- We don’t resell tokens - you use the harness subscription you already have

title.value: Show HN: Nomoreda – Browser EDA, MCP-Friendly, KiCad/Altium-Compatible

story_text.value:
Hello fellow tech workers!

My name is Andrew, cs major from University of Pittsburgh 1996 and long time BBS SysOp from 1991-1993. I grew up chatting online as a teenager. Before this new fangled internet came around, back in my day, ok sorry, to the point: Isolation and work from home jobs can drive you a little crazy.

It was always my dream before 2020. Getting the powers that be to agree to work from home. Now six years later it's definitely a careful what you wish for type situation. I got to a point with just code code code all day, interacting with no humans that I broke. Where do humans go for repair? I didn't really know. Turns out there's something called an IOP (intensive outpatient program) and yes it has the word "intensive" right in the title. Is it intense? <robert de nero voice>little bit</rdnv> But also wonderful.

All of a sudden I had a place to go Monday thru Friday and co-workers / friends! In fact, it was even better than previous office jobs because we didn't just sit next to each other on laptops and not talk, this was group therapy. I was never a fan of individual one-on-one talk therapy. But wow, group therapy is something very different.

Therapists can be incredibly helpful. Doctors can be incredibly helpful. They've spent years learning things I haven't. But they're also human. We're all flawed humans. The really interesting thing about a group is that suddenly the wisdom doesn't have to come from one person it can come from fifteen. Somebody half your age says something and you think, "OMG. They're completely right." Somebody talks about a problem that's nothing like yours, and somehow they describe exactly what you've been feeling for the last ten years. Sometimes you see somebody else describing the same ridiculous thing you've been doing, and it's much easier to recognize it when somebody ELSE does it. Sometimes the person running the group says the thing that sticks with you. Sometimes it's the guy sitting next to you eating a granola bar. There's wisdom in the group.

The site is all about helping people find, tour and enroll in your first IOP programs.

https://groupicorn.com/

https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=JhoAHUU2TCM

https://github.com/groupicorn/list-of-programs

Open source system to find all the programs in every state.

We have iphone and android app mobile apps as well. Feedback much appreciated.

title.value: Show HN: Groupicorn directory of IOP group therapy programs

Turns out there's something called an IOP (intensive outpatient program) and yes it has the word "intensive" right in the title. Is it intense? <robert de nero voice>little bit</rdnv> But also wonderful.

All of a sudden I had a place to go Monday thru Friday and co-workers / friends! In fact, it was even better than previous office jobs because we didn't just sit next to each other on laptops and not talk, this was group therapy. I was never a fan of individual one-on-one talk therapy. But wow, group therapy is something very different.

Therapists can be incredibly helpful. Doctors can be incredibly helpful. They've spent years learning things I haven't. But they're also human. We're all flawed humans. The really interesting thing about a group is that suddenly the wisdom doesn't have to come from one person it can come from fifteen. Somebody half your age says something and you think, "OMG. They're completely right." Somebody talks about a problem that's nothing like yours, and somehow they describe exactly what you've been feeling for the last ten years. Sometimes you see somebody else describing the same ridiculous thing you've been doing, and it's much easier to recognize it when somebody ELSE does it. Sometimes the person running the group says the thing that sticks with you. Sometimes it's the guy sitting next to you eating a granola bar. There's wisdom in the group.

The site is all about helping people find, tour and enroll in your first IOP programs.

We have iphone and android app mobile apps as well. Feedback much appreciated.
